title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 69–70
description: Curated B2 idioms for discussion and clear communication, plus practical English word formation with suffixes, spelling patterns and stress changes.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Checked teaching sections A–C in Unit 69 and A–D in Unit 70, all accompanying illustrations, exercises 69.1–69.3 and 70.1–70.6, language help and relevant answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA provided for straightforward words and short expressions where confidence is high; longer idioms may omit IPA. Phonemic accuracy is not exhaustively verified against an external dictionary.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Checked the uploaded source and answer-key pages, including illustrative idioms and suffix exercises, and reviewed original B2 examples, meaning, usage, register and stress-change notes. Ran JSON structural, audio-text suitability, type and ID checks; no running application tests were performed.

units.title: Unit 69 — Talking and communicating
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 144–145 (PDF pages 145–146).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Recognise idioms describing misunderstandings, interruptions and difficult communication.
Use expressions for social talk, workplace discussion, criticism and indirect communication.
Organise meetings with natural phrases for opening, focusing, summarising and finishing a discussion.
Distinguish speaking frankly, speaking sensibly and speaking in an overlong or disrespectful way.

items.pt: falar sem se entender; falar de coisas diferentes sem perceber
items.example: We were talking at cross-purposes because I meant the delivery date, not the payment date.
items.note: People misunderstand each other because they are talking about different things without realising it.

items.word: get the wrong end of the stick
items.example: I think you have got the wrong end of the stick about why the meeting was cancelled.
items.note: Means to misunderstand what was meant; get hold of the wrong end of the stick is a longer variant.

items.pt: conseguir falar; conseguir dizer alguma coisa
items.example: Everyone kept interrupting, and I could barely get a word in edgeways.
items.note: Usually appears in a negative or difficulty context; British edgeways, also edgewise.

items.word: can't make head or tail of it
items.pt: não conseguir entender nada; não fazer ideia do que significa
items.example: The manual is so confusing that I can't make head or tail of it.
items.note: Typically can't make head or tail of something; signals complete inability to understand it.

items.pt: falar com superioridade; tratar com condescendência
items.example: Please don't talk down to the trainees when explaining the procedure.
items.note: Speak as if someone is less intelligent or important than you.

items.pt: falar mal de mim pelas costas
items.example: I would rather hear your concerns directly than have you talk behind my back.
items.note: Change my to his, her or their when referring to other people; generally suggests negative remarks.

items.pt: conversa fiada; conversa informal de circunstância
items.example: A little small talk helped everyone feel comfortable before the interview.
items.note: Light social conversation rather than a serious discussion; usually uncountable.

items.pt: falar de trabalho fora do expediente
items.example: We agreed not to talk shop during dinner with our friends.
items.note: Informal idiom for discussing work when socialising with colleagues.

items.pt: assunto do momento; tema muito comentado
items.example: The proposed change has become a talking point across the department.
items.note: A subject that attracts attention and discussion.

items.example: The manager gave him a talking-to for ignoring the safety rules.
items.note: Informal countable noun; commonly give someone a talking-to.

items.pt: dar início; começar a discussão ou atividade
items.example: Could you start the ball rolling by explaining the main objective?
items.note: Begin an activity or discussion so others can contribute.

items.example: To put it in a nutshell, we need more testing before the product is ready.
items.note: Express the essential point briefly; often introduced by to put it in a nutshell.

items.example: We only have ten minutes, so let's get to the point.
items.note: Stop giving unnecessary details and address the important issue; come to the point is a variant.

items.pt: dizer o que penso; falar francamente
items.example: I decided to speak my mind about the unrealistic deadline.
items.note: Express your genuine opinion openly; change the possessive with the subject.

items.pt: encerrar a discussão; concluir o debate
items.example: We should wrap up the discussion and agree on the next actions.
items.note: Wrap up means bring a meeting, debate or other activity to an end.

items.pt: falar coisas sensatas; falar com bom senso
items.example: Maya always talks sense when we discuss technical risks.
items.note: Say reasonable, intelligent things; contrasted with talk rubbish.

items.example: He was talking rubbish when he claimed that the test required no preparation.
items.note: Informal, dismissive British phrase for saying silly or untrue things.

items.pt: prolixo; que se alonga demais para explicar
items.example: His long-winded explanation confused the audience instead of helping them.
items.note: Describes speech or writing that takes too long to make its point.

sectionsChecked: A: Four illustrated idioms for communication problems and their explanatory glosses
B: Social and workplace expressions for positive and negative talk
C: Eight illustrated expressions for handling discussions and meetings
Exercises 69.1–69.3, visual prompts and Unit 69 answer key

units.title: Unit 70 — Suffixes
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 146–147 (PDF pages 147–148).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Identify common noun-forming endings for people, objects, actions and abstract concepts.
Distinguish agent suffixes from recipient suffixes, especially -er and -ee.
Form and recognise adjectives and verbs using productive English suffix patterns.
Notice spelling and word-stress changes when a suffix is attached to a base word.
Recognise less precise informal descriptions formed with -ish.

items.example: The writer interviewed several experts before publishing her article.
items.note: Write becomes writer with -er: someone who performs the activity.

items.example: The supervisor checks that every operator follows the safety procedures.
items.note: Supervise becomes supervisor; -or is an alternative spelling of the agent ending.

items.example: The machine operator reported an unusual vibration.
items.note: An -or noun for the person operating a machine or system.

items.example: The donor agreed to contribute equipment to the research centre.
items.note: A donor gives something, such as money, organs or equipment.

items.example: There is a pencil sharpener in the top drawer.
items.note: -er can describe a device that performs an action, not only a person.

items.example: Use a can opener to open the tin without spilling anything.
items.note: Tin opener is another common British name for this kitchen tool.

items.example: I borrowed a stapler to fasten the printed handouts.
items.note: A tool for attaching sheets of paper with staples.

items.example: Use a fine grater for the lemon peel.
items.note: A kitchen tool whose name uses the instrument suffix -er.

items.example: The projector stopped working halfway through the presentation.
items.note: An -or noun for equipment that projects images.

items.example: I left my jacket on a coat hanger near the door.
items.note: Hanger comes from hang and names an object used for hanging something.

items.example: The windscreen wiper needs replacing before the rainy season.
items.note: A wiper removes water; windscreen is British English for a car's front glass.

items.pt: profissional de limpeza; aparelho de limpeza
items.example: The cleaner arrived before the office opened.
items.note: Can mean a person who cleans or a machine/product that cleans, depending on context.

items.pt: portador de ingresso; suporte para bilhete
items.example: Every ticket holder must present identification at the entrance.
items.note: Can refer to the person holding a ticket or an object used to hold tickets.

items.pt: máquina de lavar louça; pessoa que lava louça
items.example: The dishwasher finishes its cycle in about an hour.
items.note: Names a machine or a person who washes dishes; in this example it is a machine.

items.example: The employer provided additional safety training.
items.note: The employer employs another person; contrast with employee, the person employed.

items.example: Every employee must complete the induction course.
items.note: -ee marks the person employed by another person or organisation; compare employer.

items.example: The sender forgot to include the order number on the parcel.
items.note: A sender sends something; compare addressee, who receives a message.

items.example: The addressee's name is missing from the envelope.
items.note: The person to whom a message or letter is addressed; -ee does not always simply mean employee-like status.

items.example: Please check the payee before authorising the bank transfer.
items.note: A person or organisation to whom money is paid; contrast payer.

items.example: Traffic pollution is a major concern in large cities.
items.note: Pollute becomes pollution; -tion commonly forms a noun from a verb.

items.example: The design resulted in a reduction in power consumption.
items.note: Reduce becomes reduction; notice the change from -ce to -ction.

items.example: Her promotion to team leader was announced yesterday.
items.note: Promote becomes promotion; can refer to career advancement or advertising.

items.example: Admission to the laboratory requires prior authorisation.
items.note: Admit becomes admission with a consonant and spelling change; not admittion.

items.example: The team agreed on a course of action after reviewing the results.
items.note: Related to act; notice -ion in action and -ive in active.

items.example: A physicist explained the detector's operating principle.
items.note: -ist can identify people in a profession or specialised area.

items.example: The pianist performed a short piece at the concert.
items.note: A performer who plays the piano; notice the change in stress from piano to pianist.

items.example: The violinist joined the orchestra last year.
items.note: -ist identifies a player of a musical instrument; compare pianist and cellist.

items.example: The article examines several Marxist ideas about economic history.
items.note: -ist can name a person associated with a political or philosophical tradition and can also be an adjective.

items.example: The course introduces students to the history of Buddhism in Asia.
items.note: -ism can form the name of a belief or religious tradition; capitalise Buddhism.

items.example: She studied journalism before working for a regional newspaper.
items.note: -ism can form the name of a field or activity, not only an ideology.

items.example: The engineer checked the team's readiness for the next test.
items.note: Ready becomes readiness; the final -y changes to -i before -ness.

items.example: Long-term happiness depends on more than income alone.
items.note: Happy becomes happiness; -y changes to -i.

items.example: His forgetfulness sometimes causes minor scheduling problems.
items.note: Derived from forgetful + -ness; describes the tendency to forget.

items.example: Laziness was not the issue; she simply needed clearer instructions.
items.note: Lazy becomes laziness; the exercise checks the y-to-i spelling change.

items.example: These berries are edible, but the ones on the other bush are poisonous.
items.note: Means safe or suitable to eat; the spelling uses -ible.

items.example: We need a flexible schedule while the prototype is being developed.
items.note: Can bend, or adapt to changes; compare flexibility in section D.

items.example: A small typing mistake is forgivable, but falsifying results is not.
items.note: Forgive becomes forgivable; -able can mean able to be acted on.

items.example: The updated instructions are much more readable than the old version.
items.note: Read becomes readable; used for text that is clear or easy to read.

items.example: This jacket is machine washable at low temperatures.
items.note: Wash becomes washable; the -able adjective describes what can be washed.

items.example: The tap water is drinkable after filtration.
items.note: Formed from drink; means suitable or safe to drink.

items.example: The company plans to modernise its quality-control procedures.
items.note: Makes something modern; modernize is an alternative spelling common in American English.

items.example: Researchers hope to commercialise the new sensor next year.
items.note: Formed from commercial; commercialize is another spelling.

items.example: The museum decided to computerise its paper records.
items.note: Make a process computer-based; computerize is another spelling.

items.example: The replacement of the damaged board took two hours.
items.note: Replace becomes replacement; can mean the act or the substitute itself.

items.example: Reading in English brings her a great deal of enjoyment.
items.note: Enjoy becomes enjoyment; -ment forms a noun for a state or result.

items.example: The flexible arrangement gives the team greater flexibility.
items.note: Related to flexible; stress moves from the first to the fourth syllable.

items.example: Better tools can improve productivity without increasing working hours.
items.note: From productive; primary stress shifts to -tiv- in productivity.

items.example: Water scarcity threatens agriculture in the region.
items.note: From scarce, meaning insufficient availability; note the resulting spelling.

items.example: She spent most of her childhood near the coast.
items.note: -hood forms nouns describing a period or state.

items.example: She wrote about the challenges of motherhood and working life.
items.note: -hood forms a state or experience related to a family role.

items.example: Their friendship continued after they moved to different cities.
items.note: -ship forms a noun describing a relationship or status.

items.example: The club offers discounted membership to students.
items.note: A state of belonging to a group; also refers to all its members collectively.

items.example: We had a productive meeting and agreed on three actions.
items.note: From produce; compare productivity, with a different stress pattern.

items.example: The device remains active throughout the measurement.
items.note: Related to act; -ive is a common adjective ending.

items.example: The report was written in the passive voice.
items.note: Can describe a non-active participant or a grammatical construction.

items.example: The contract was reviewed by the legal department.
items.note: The -al ending makes an adjective describing something related to or permitted by law.

items.example: Her refusal to approve the request delayed the project.
items.note: Refuse becomes refusal; -al sometimes forms nouns rather than adjectives.

items.example: We expect the equipment's arrival on Monday.
items.note: Arrive becomes arrival; another example of noun-forming -al.

items.example: The supplier charged an outrageous price for a simple repair.
items.note: Describes something shockingly unreasonable or unacceptable.

items.example: She was furious when she discovered the repeated errors.
items.note: Derived from fury; stronger than merely annoyed.

items.example: The homemade meal was absolutely delicious.
items.note: An adjective with -ous describing a very pleasant taste.

items.example: He is forgetful, so he keeps a written checklist.
items.note: Describes a person who often forgets; compare forgetfulness.

items.example: The researchers are hopeful that the second trial will succeed.
items.note: Hope + -ful describes a positive expectation.

items.example: The insect is harmless to humans.
items.note: -less means without; harmless means not likely to cause harm.

items.example: The old cable is useless because its connector is broken.
items.note: Opposite of useful; -less often expresses absence of something.

items.example: The charity provides emergency accommodation for homeless people.
items.note: Without a home; may describe people living without secure housing.

items.example: The council plans to beautify the public square.
items.note: From beauty; -ify means make something have a quality.

items.example: The laboratory uses filters to purify the water.
items.note: Make something pure by removing unwanted substances.

items.example: The sudden noise might terrify a small child.
items.note: Means to make someone extremely frightened; stronger than worry.

items.example: The new instructor looks thirtyish.
items.note: Informal -ish suggests an approximate age; not an exact value.

items.example: The metal developed a reddish colour after heating.
items.note: Red + -ish means somewhat red; an approximate colour description, without naming a precise shade.

items.example: We can meet at eightish if the train is on time.
items.note: Informal -ish added to a time means approximately, not exactly.

items.example: The photographer checked the lighting before taking the portrait.
items.note: An -er person noun; compare photograph, whose stress falls on a different syllable.

B: Possibility and ability adjectives with -able and -ible
Language help: stress shifts in related word families
